source: Rewritten from AI-DEMO2 buildTraceSteps STEP_SPEC (2026-11-08) plus new entries; no identifiers.

spec.mandate: OAuth issues the user token only after the user authenticates; how the credentials are collected is up to the authorization server. This lab signs in with a pi.flow: the page drives the sign-in in place, with no redirect, and the code is still redeemed with PKCE.
spec.why: The lab hands the user token to the page so you can follow it through every hop. A production app keeps it in the back end and gives the browser only a session cookie.
spec.failure: Keeping the user token in browser storage in a real app. Any script on the page can then lift the subject token, and every delegation check later in the chain proves nothing.

spec.mandate: RFC 8693 defines may_act: a claim on the subject token that names who is allowed to act for the subject. The authorization server checks it before it issues a delegated token.
spec.why: Consent is recorded as data the authorization server can enforce, not as a checkbox in the app. If the customer never consented, the exchange later in the chain is refused.
spec.failure: Recording consent only in the app. The authorization server then delegates to any agent that asks, and the consent screen is decoration.

spec.mandate: Client credentials issue a token for the client itself, with no user in it. The JWT access token profile names that machine principal in client_id and sub.
spec.why: The agent needs its own provable identity, so the next exchange has a real actor_token to present. Without it there is no evidence of who acted, only that a call arrived.
spec.failure: Using the user token as the agent identity. The user and the agent collapse into one party, and the act claim made next proves nothing.

spec.mandate: The client posts grant_type token-exchange with subject_token (the user) and actor_token (the agent). The new token keeps sub as the user and puts the agent in act.sub. The resource parameter pins its audience.
spec.why: One token now carries both parties, so every later hop can see who is acted for and who is acting. Scope is cut to what the tool needs and the audience is pinned, so the token is useless anywhere else.
spec.failure: Asking for the same broad scope the user already has, which keeps the delegation but loses least privilege. Or leaving out resource, so any service that trusts the issuer accepts the token.

spec.mandate: An ordinary RFC 8693 exchange: the first agent becomes the actor for the customer, recorded in act.
spec.why: The chain starts with one actor so the next agent can be added under it and every hop stays attributable.
spec.failure: Skipping this step and letting the second agent call with the customer token directly. Nothing then shows which agent passed the job on.

spec.mandate: RFC 8693 records a chain of actors as nested act claims, with the most recent actor outermost.
spec.why: Each hand-off narrows scope and adds the next agent, so the specialist can do only its part and the whole chain is visible in one token.
spec.failure: Copying the first agent token to the second agent. The specialist then holds more than it needs and the chain shows one actor instead of two.

spec.mandate: A protected resource rejects a bad token with 401 and a WWW-Authenticate challenge. A JWT access token is checked for signature, audience, expiry and scope; an opaque one is introspected.
spec.why: The gateway is the one place every agent call passes. It checks signature, audience, expiry, scope and the act chain, so a tool is never the only thing between a forged token and the data.
spec.failure: Checking the signature but not the audience. A correctly signed token minted for another service still passes, so a stolen token works anywhere.

refs.label: XACML 3.0
refs.title: Decision point and enforcement point vocabulary

refs.label: RFC 8693 §4.1
refs.title: act chain as a policy attribute

spec.mandate: No RFC defines the decision itself; it is attribute-based access control. The enforcement point sends subject, actor, action, resource and context to a decision point and obeys PERMIT, DENY or a step-up. The act claim (RFC 8693 §4.1) is one of the attributes it reads.
spec.why: Policy runs before the tool, in one place a security team can change without redeploying the agent. Each verdict has a decision id, so it can be audited.
spec.failure: Assuming a DENY came from your rule. A DENY proves the engine answered, not which rule fired; check the decision id against the rule you expected.

spec.mandate: tools/call sends the tool name and schema-checked arguments over JSON-RPC. Under MCP authorization the server is an OAuth resource server and checks the bearer itself.
spec.why: The MCP server checks the token again instead of trusting the gateway, so a bug at the gateway does not become open data access.
spec.failure: Trusting a user id the gateway put in a header. Anything that can reach the MCP server directly can then pretend to be any user.

refs.label: XACML 3.0
refs.title: Decision point and enforcement point vocabulary

spec.mandate: A decision can carry an obligation, such as a human approval, that must be met before the action runs.
spec.why: The write is held at the gateway, so nothing reaches the tool until the obligation is met. The agent can explain why it is waiting.
spec.failure: Treating the obligation as advice. If the caller can skip it, the hold does not exist; check that the call really stopped.

spec.mandate: A refused call never reaches the resource. A bad or expired token gets 401 invalid_token; a valid token without the needed scope gets 403 insufficient_scope.
spec.why: The refusal happens before the tool, so no tool code runs and nothing is half done.
spec.failure: Reading an expected refusal as an outage. In a deny use case the refusal is the control working.

spec.mandate: Only actors the policy allows may appear in the act chain; an unknown actor is refused.
spec.why: An agent that is not registered tries to join the chain, to show that the gateway checks every actor, not just the last one.
spec.failure: Checking only the outermost actor. An unknown agent hidden deeper in the chain then gets through.

spec.mandate: A2A calls are HTTP calls; the caller authenticates with the scheme the agent card declares, here a bearer token.
spec.why: The delegated token with the nested act chain travels with the A2A call, so the receiving agent knows who it works for.
spec.failure: Calling the other agent with the first agent's own token. The receiver then cannot tell which customer the work is for.

spec.mandate: An A2A agent publishes an agent card describing its skills, endpoint and the authentication it requires.
spec.why: The caller reads the card to learn how to authenticate before it sends any work.
spec.failure: Trusting a card fetched from anywhere. A hostile card can point the caller at the wrong endpoint; pin or verify the card.

spec.mandate: message/send (A2A 0.3; earlier drafts called it tasks/send) carries the task to the other agent as an A2A message.
spec.why: The job moves to the specialist with the delegated token attached, so the specialist acts within the narrowed scope.
spec.failure: Putting the customer data in the message without a token. The specialist then has data but no proof it may act on it.

spec.mandate: CIBA starts a decoupled sign-in: the client asks the authorization server to reach the user on a separate device.
spec.why: The customer is brought back in at the moment of risk, on their own phone, without the agent ever seeing their credentials.
spec.failure: Sending the approval request with too little binding text. The customer then approves something they cannot recognise.

spec.mandate: The client polls the token endpoint until the user decides. The token records how the user signed in (amr).
spec.why: The approval is evidence: the new token says a person approved, how, and when.
spec.failure: Polling too fast or ignoring slow_down. The server can then throttle the client and the approval looks lost.

spec.why: The gateway checks the signed approval receipt before it releases the held write, so the approval cannot be faked by the agent.
spec.failure: Accepting an approval the agent reports itself. The agent can then approve its own risky action.

spec.mandate: PAR sends the authorization request, with RAR authorization_details, straight to the authorization server on the back channel.
spec.why: The declared intent (payee and cap) never rides in a browser URL, so nothing in between can read or change it.
spec.failure: Treating a successful push as an approval. PAR only stores the request; nothing has been checked yet.

spec.mandate: RAR replaces broad scope with structured details: type, actions and limits such as a maximum amount or a target account.
spec.why: The call is checked against what the customer declared, not against what the agent says at call time.
spec.failure: Assuming the authorization server enforced the amount. If it never parsed the limit, an over-cap call sails through while the flow looks correct.

spec.mandate: A bearer token is meant for its audience only; passing it on unchanged hands the user full authority to the next party.
spec.why: This hop shows the anti-pattern on purpose: the back end forwards the user token without an exchange, and the gateway refuses it.
spec.failure: Forwarding the user token to the agent or tool. There is no act claim, so nobody can tell the agent from the customer.

spec.mandate: The agent presents its bearer to the agent gateway, which decides allow, deny or hold for each tool call.
spec.why: Every tool call from the agent passes one enforcement point that knows the agent identity.
spec.failure: Letting the agent call tools directly. Nothing then records or limits what it does.

spec.mandate: No specification covers this hop: it is where OAuth ends. The gateway drops the caller bearer and attaches the operator credential.
spec.why: Back-end systems that cannot check OAuth still never receive the caller token, so a compromised system holds only a rotatable service credential.
spec.failure: Forwarding both the bearer and the service credential. The back end then holds a token it has no reason to have.

spec.mandate: In the enterprise profile the identity provider evaluates policy before it issues any credential for an MCP server.
spec.why: IT decides in one place which people reach which MCP servers, and revoking access takes effect on the next call.
spec.failure: Deciding after the credential exists. Every service then has to remember to refuse it, and one that forgets is the hole.

spec.mandate: An RFC 8693 exchange asks for token type id-jag, with audience set to the MCP authorization server. The assertion is a typed JWT with jti, iss, sub, aud, resource and scope.
spec.why: Policy runs at the identity provider before any token exists, so a person who is not entitled never receives anything to present.
spec.failure: Checking policy after the assertion is minted. That is downstream enforcement, not central control.

spec.mandate: The jwt-bearer grant presents the ID-JAG. The MCP authorization server checks signature, issuer, audience, expiry and resource, then issues its own token for that MCP server.
spec.why: The MCP authorization server stays the issuer of its own tokens instead of trusting a foreign one.
spec.failure: Accepting an unpinned algorithm or a reused jti. A forged or replayed assertion then grants everything.

spec.mandate: A signed JWT assertion states facts about the agent that a receiver can verify against the issuer key.
spec.why: The receiving agent can verify who the delegating agent is before it accepts the work.
spec.failure: Accepting an assertion without checking its issuer key. Any agent can then claim to be trusted.

spec.why: The workload agent is looked up in the agent registry, so only registered, owned agents can act.
spec.failure: Letting an agent act because it presented a name. Without a registry check any process can claim to be the agent.

spec.why: This use case is a learning page; the lab opens it and the product shows its own demo.
spec.failure: Presenting a guide as a computed result. Nothing here was decided by the engine.

spec.mandate: An authorization server publishes its metadata (issuer, endpoints, supported grants) at a well-known URL, and a client reads it instead of hard-coding them.
spec.why: Whether this environment supports token exchange is read from grant_types_supported, not assumed.
spec.failure: Hard-coding endpoints or assuming a grant is supported. The demo then fails later with a confusing error instead of saying the feature is off.

spec.mandate: Client credentials issue a token for the client itself, with no user in it. The JWT access token profile names that machine principal in client_id and sub.
spec.why: The agent needs its own provable identity, so the next exchange has a real actor_token to present. Without it there is no evidence of who acted, only that a call arrived.
spec.failure: Using the user token as the agent identity. The user and the agent collapse into one party, and the act claim made next proves nothing.

spec.why: The browser hosts the page and holds no bearer token. The back end for the front end (BFF) knows the user by an HttpOnly session cookie that page scripts cannot read; OpenID Connect and PKCE assume the tokens stay on the server.
spec.failure: Keeping access tokens in browser storage. Any script on the page, including an injected one, can then read them and replay them from elsewhere.

spec.why: The browser sends only the customer's words to the BFF. The session cookie says who is asking; no Authorization header leaves the page.
spec.failure: Sending a bearer token with the chat message. The token then sits in the page, in logs and in every proxy on the way.

spec.why: The BFF hands the request to the agent, which works out what the customer wants and which tool could do it. In this lab the agent's brain is a scripted intent match, not a model.
spec.failure: Letting the agent act on the request before any identity is attached. Every later check then has nothing to check against.

spec.mandate: A protected resource answers a request with no token with 401 and a WWW-Authenticate challenge. RFC 9728 adds resource_metadata: the URL of a document that names the resource and the authorization servers it trusts. MCP authorization uses exactly this to tell a client where to get a token.
spec.why: The first tools/list carries no credential on purpose. The gateway refuses it and points at its metadata, which is how a client that holds nothing learns which authorization server to use. A 401 is the expected result here.
spec.failure: Answering an anonymous tools/list with the full tool catalog. Anyone who can reach the gateway then learns every tool and its arguments without signing in.

spec.mandate: An MCP session starts with initialize and notifications/initialized; the client then asks tools/list for the tools it may call. Under MCP authorization the request carries a bearer token for the gateway.
spec.why: The second tools/list carries a token, so the catalog can be filtered to what this caller may use. The model only ever sees tools the policy would allow.
spec.failure: Showing the model every tool and relying on the call-time check alone. The model then plans calls that will be refused, and the full catalog leaks to every caller.

spec.why: The agent's model reads the request and proposes a tool call. It never sees or holds an OAuth token: the model proposes, policy decides. In this lab the model is a scripted intent match (mock).
spec.failure: Treating the model's choice as permission. A prompt can steer any model, so the decision has to come from the policy and the gateway, not from the plan.

spec.mandate: The same challenge on invocation: a tools/call with no bearer gets 401 and a WWW-Authenticate header that names the resource metadata.
spec.why: It shows the gateway refuses an unauthenticated invocation before anything runs. Nothing executes on this leg; the authorized call follows with the delegated token.
spec.failure: Running the tool and checking the token afterwards. A call with no credential then has side effects before the refusal arrives.

api-call.title: Resource server
api-call.fact: API called with the delegated token

spec.mandate: The tool reaches the back-end API with the delegated access token in the Authorization header. The API is a resource server and answers insufficient_scope when the token does not cover the request.
spec.why: The resource server checks the delegated token itself, so the data comes back only for the customer and scope that token names.
spec.failure: Calling the API with a shared service credential and passing the user id alongside. The API then cannot tell which customer really asked, and one bug exposes every account.

spec.why: The agent turns the tool result into the reply the customer reads. The reply carries data, never a token.
spec.failure: Echoing raw tool output or headers into the chat. Anything sensitive in the result, a token included, then lands on the screen and in the transcript.

spec.mandate: When policy asks for more assurance, the customer approves again: a second factor, an approval on another device (CIBA) or a person in the loop. The token then records how they authenticated (amr).
spec.why: A risky write waits until the human approves it. The agent cannot approve on the customer's behalf.
spec.failure: Accepting an "approved" flag sent by the client. Anything that can post that flag skips the approval entirely.

spec.why: On the API-key path the gateway fetches the key bound to this tool route from a vault. The key stays on the server and is shown masked.
spec.failure: Putting the service key in the agent or the page. Whoever reads it can call the back end directly, with no user and no policy.

api-key-swap.title: API-key swap
api-key-swap.fact: bearer swapped for a service key

spec.mandate: A bearer token is meant for its audience only. When the downstream service takes an API key instead, the gateway drops the bearer and sends the service key plus the user's subject.
spec.why: The user's bearer never travels past the gateway, and the back end still learns which user the call is for.
spec.failure: Forwarding the user's bearer to a service it was not issued for. That service can now replay it anywhere the token is accepted.

spec.why: The back-end application reads its own data store to answer the call. Only the back end talks to the database; no token reaches it.
spec.failure: Letting the tool or the agent query the database directly. Every access rule enforced in the API is then bypassed.
